claims.claim: It's four in the morning, December fourteenth, two thousand five.
claims.reason: Timeline events indicate the incident began around 04:39 on December 14, 2005.

claims.claim: In the Ozark mountains of Missouri, a park superintendent's house sits at the foot of Proffit Mountain.
claims.reason: Stakeholders identify Jerry Toops as the Johnson's Shut-Ins State Park superintendent and his house at the foot of Proffit Mountain.

claims.claim: Jerry Toops is asleep. His wife Lisa is awake with the baby. Three children.
claims.reason: Stakeholders list Jerry, Lisa, and three children (Tanner, Tara, Tucker) and timeline events describe Lisa awake with the baby when the flood hit.

claims.claim: A quarter of a mile above their roof, on the flattened top of the mountain, sits a lake.
claims.reason: The upper reservoir is described as on Proffit Mountain, above Johnson's Shut-Ins State Park.

claims.claim: A man-made ring of rock and concrete
claims.reason: Stakeholders describe the upper reservoir as a 'mountaintop rockfill ring with a settled concrete parapet'.

claims.claim: holding one and a half billion gallons of water.
claims.reason: Data points state the reservoir held '~4,350 acre-feet (~1.4 billion gallons)', making 'one and a half billion' an inflation.

claims.claim: a computer ninety miles away has been pumping more water in.
claims.reason: Data points and stakeholders confirm the plant was operated by remote control from St. Louis, ~90 miles away, and pumping continued into the early morning of the breach.

claims.claim: At five fifteen, Lisa hears it.
claims.reason: Timeline events state the flood wave hit the Toops home between ~05:15-05:20.

claims.claim: A roar, like jet engines and freight trains at once.
claims.reason: Jerry Toops is quoted in stakeholders describing the wave as 'a group of F-14 jets combined with a fleet of trains'.

claims.claim: The house fills with black winter water in seconds. The walls come apart.
claims.reason: Timeline events state the house filled in seconds and FERC p. 134 notes the house was destroyed.

claims.claim: And the whole family — Jerry, Lisa, a five-year-old, a three-year-old, a seven-month-old baby — is swept into the dark.
claims.reason: Stakeholders confirm all five Toops family members (Jerry, Lisa, Tanner (5), Tara (3), Tucker (7 months)) were swept ~1/4 mile.

claims.claim: One and a half billion gallons emptied through the valley in twenty-five minutes.
claims.reason: Data points state the reservoir released '~4,350 acre-feet (~1.4 billion gallons)' in '~25 minutes', making the volume an inflation.

claims.claim: Nobody at the plant pressed a wrong button. Nobody fell asleep at a control panel.
claims.reason: Data points and stakeholders confirm the plant was operated by remote control from St. Louis, with manual shutdown instructions coming from St. Louis to Bagnell Dam.

claims.claim: There was no control panel.
claims.reason: Deep extraction notes the control architecture included a 'WonderWare Operator Interface for level indication, alarming, and data acquisition', which is a control interface, even if not a manned operational panel.

claims.claim: There was a computer, reading sensors that had been wrong for months — and everyone knew.
claims.reason: Deep extraction and timeline events show a software offset was added in Sept 2005 due to visual observations disagreeing with instruments, and employees observed transducer movement and gauge disagreement for months.

claims.claim: Taum Sauk was a battery. Not a chemical one — a battery made of water and gravity.
claims.reason: The research brief topic identifies Taum Sauk as a 'pumped-storage plant', which functions as a water-and-gravity battery.

claims.claim: At night, when electricity is cheap, giant pumps push water from a river up the mountain into the reservoir.
claims.reason: This is a standard description of the pumping cycle for a pumped-storage hydroelectric facility, consistent with the brief's context.

claims.claim: In the day, when demand peaks, the water falls back down through turbines and becomes electricity again.
claims.reason: This is a standard description of the generation cycle for a pumped-storage hydroelectric facility, consistent with the brief's context.

claims.claim: The upper reservoir was a ring of rockfill crowning the mountain, topped with a concrete wall.
claims.reason: Stakeholders describe the upper reservoir as a 'mountaintop rockfill ring with a settled concrete parapet'.

claims.claim: It held four thousand three hundred fifty acre-feet of water.
claims.reason: Data points explicitly state the reservoir held '~4,350 acre-feet'.

claims.claim: And it had one unusual feature: no spillway. No overflow drain.
claims.reason: Data points explicitly state 'The upper reservoir had NO emergency spillway'.

claims.claim: If the water ever rose too high, there was nowhere for it to go — except over the wall, and through it.
claims.reason: Data points explain that 'overtopping meant erosion of the rockfill, by design a fatal condition' due to the lack of a spillway.

claims.claim: Nobody worked on the mountain.
claims.reason: FERC p. 103 and IPOC p. 16 indicate plant superintendent Richard Cooper was on site the morning of the breach.

claims.claim: The plant ran by remote control from Saint Louis, ninety miles away.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 16 confirms remote operation from St. Louis ~90 miles away.

claims.claim: The computer's eyes were four pressure sensors under the water, riding in plastic pipes on the reservoir floor.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 14 and p. 21 state TX1 transducer was removed from service on Sept 27, 2005, leaving fewer than four.

claims.claim: In two thousand four, those pipes had been replaced
claims.reason: Timeline event 2004-11 confirms new instrumentation installed in 2004.

claims.claim: the new ones were never anchored down.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 8, 109 and timeline event 2004-11 confirm the conduits were not anchored.

claims.claim: As backup, five simple probes hung near the top of the wall
claims.reason: IPOC p. 15 and timeline event 2004-11 confirm five Warrick probes as backup.

claims.claim: bare metal switches that close when water touches them.
claims.reason: General knowledge of Warrick conductivity probes confirms this operational principle.

claims.claim: The very top one and the very bottom one were wired to kill the pumps.
claims.reason: FERC p. 63 confirms LO-LO and HI-HI probes were wired to hard-stop the units.

claims.claim: The ones between were wired to nothing.
claims.reason: FERC p. 63 states LO and HI probes were wired but configured not to alarm or log, not 'wired to nothing.'

claims.claim: If water reached them, no alarm would sound.
claims.reason: FERC p. 63 confirms LO and HI probes would not generate an alarm.

claims.claim: The computer wouldn't even write it down.
claims.reason: FERC p. 63 confirms the PLC historian would not record water touching LO and HI probes.

claims.claim: The wall had been sinking since the day it was built.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 11 and timeline event 1963 confirm settlement began with first filling in 1963.

claims.claim: Rockfill settles.
claims.reason: General engineering knowledge about rockfill dam construction.

claims.claim: By two thousand five, parts of the parapet had dropped a full foot.
claims.reason: FERC p. 14 and IPOC p. 11 confirm the wall settled about one foot.

claims.claim: the depth gauge the staff read was bolted to that same wall.
claims.reason: FERC p. 14 and IPOC p. 11 confirm the staff gage was affixed to the parapet wall.

claims.claim: The wall sank. The gauge sank with it.
claims.reason: FERC p. 14 and IPOC p. 11 confirm the staff gage settled with the wall.

claims.claim: The numbers looked perfect.
claims.reason: FERC p. 14 and IPOC p. 11 state the staff gage settled with the wall, making the numbers appear normal.

claims.claim: September twenty-fifth, two thousand five.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 55 and timeline event 2005-09-25 confirm the date.

claims.claim: Eighty days before the breach.
claims.reason: Calculation from timeline events 2005-09-25 and 2005-12-14.

claims.claim: After the rains of Hurricane Rita
claims.reason: IPOC p. 55 and timeline event 2005-09-25 confirm this occurred after Hurricane Rita rains.

claims.claim: workers on the mountain watch water pouring over the northwest corner of the wall.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 55 and timeline event 2005-09-25 confirm workers witnessed overtopping at the northwest corner.

claims.claim: One of them will describe it as Niagara Falls.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 55 and timeline event 2005-09-25 confirm this description.

claims.claim: They save the dam by hand — slamming the plant into generate to drain the reservoir down.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 55 and timeline event 2005-09-25 confirm units were manually switched to generate mode.

claims.claim: Two days later, an engineer writes it down in an email
claims.reason: IPOC p. 55 and timeline event 2005-09-27 confirm an internal email dated 9/27/2005 documented the near-miss.

claims.claim: overflowing this reservoir is, quote, an absolute no-no.
claims.reason: The exact quote "overflowing this reservoir is, quote, an absolute no-no" is not found in the research brief.

claims.claim: The water will erode the dam, and the dam will fail.
claims.reason: ASDSO case study and IPOC design sections confirm the dam had no emergency spillway, making overtopping a fatal condition.

claims.claim: It is dated September twenty-seventh
claims.reason: IPOC p. 55 and timeline event 2005-09-27 confirm the email date.

claims.claim: eleven weeks before it happened.
claims.reason: Calculation from timeline events 2005-09-27 and 2005-12-14 confirms approximately 11 weeks.

claims.claim: The plant knew the pipes had moved.
claims.reason: Timeline event 2005-10 to 12 confirms employees observed movement of the HDPE conduits.

claims.claim: The readings disagreed with what people could see with their own eyes.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 14, 21 confirm the software offset was added in response to visual observations disagreeing with instruments.

claims.claim: So on September twenty-seventh, someone fixed it — in software.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 14, 21 and timeline event 2005-09-27 confirm a software offset was added on Sept 27, 2005.

claims.claim: They typed a correction into the computer: add point four feet.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 14, 21 and timeline event 2005-09-27 confirm a 0.4 ft software offset was added.

claims.claim: Don't re-anchor the pipes.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 8, 109 state the pipes were never anchored, not that a decision was made not to re-anchor them.

claims.claim: Don't drain and repair.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 14, 21 indicate a software patch was applied instead of a physical sensor repair.

claims.claim: Just… adjust the number.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 14, 21 confirm a 0.4 ft software offset was added to the PLC code.

claims.claim: October seventh. Another email.
claims.reason: Timeline event 2005-10-07 confirms an internal email on this date.

claims.claim: the emergency probes sit seven inches, and four inches, from the top of the wall.
claims.reason: Deep extraction and timeline event for 2005-10-07 explicitly state this.

claims.claim: During the September spill, the water must have reached them.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 25 email implies water reached the level of the probes during the 9/25 near-miss overtopping.

claims.claim: They should have tripped.
claims.reason: The 10/07 email states 'the Hi level Warrick should have picked up'.

claims.claim: They didn't.
claims.reason: The 10/07 email implies the Hi level Warrick did not pick up, and the dam later breached.

claims.claim: The email even offers: we can lower the probes if you want.
claims.reason: Deep extraction for 10/07 email quotes: 'If you want to lower the Hi level probes we can do that'.

claims.claim: The reply history shows what happened next. Nothing.
claims.reason: Deep extraction for 10/07 email states Ameren 'discussed and declined lowering the fail-safe setpoints'.

claims.claim: Early December. The plant superintendent walks the wall on a routine morning and sees wet spots on the outside of the parapet — at its lowest point.
claims.reason: Brief states 'pre-breach morning visit' for Cooper's observation, not specifically 'Early December'.

claims.claim: Spray, probably. Waves.
claims.reason: FERC p. 112 states Cooper's observation was 'possibly spray from waves'.

claims.claim: It was explainable.
claims.reason: FERC p. 112 states 'the observation that SHOULD have been a red flag was explainable-away in the moment'.

claims.claim: The pumps kept their schedule.
claims.reason: Timeline 2005-10 to 12 states 'plant keeps operating on remote control from St. Louis'.

claims.claim: The sensors, riding in their loose pipes, are reading four point two feet low.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 19 and data point confirm sensors read ~4.2 ft low; IPOC pp. 8, 109 confirm loose pipes.

claims.claim: The computer in Saint Louis believes the water is six feet below the top.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 16 states indicated level was 1591.6 ft, meaning 5.4 ft below the 1597 ft wall, not 'six feet'.

claims.claim: The probes that would catch the lie are set above the lowest point of the sinking wall
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 16, 19-20 and data point confirm Hi-Hi probe at 1597.70 ft, 0.7 ft above the 1597 ft lowest wall point; IPOC p. 11 confirms wall settlement.

claims.claim: the middle ones wouldn't say anything anyway.
claims.reason: FERC p. 63 states the LO and HI probes would NOT generate an alarm or log.

claims.claim: The emergency stop — the last line of defense — was set seven tenths of a foot above the lowest point of the wall.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 16, 19-20 and data point confirm Hi-Hi probe at 1597.70 ft, 0.7 ft ABOVE the 1597 ft lowest wall point.

claims.claim: Water would be pouring over the dam before the machine was allowed to notice.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 16, 19-20 states 'Water physically overtopped the dam before the emergency stop could ever trigger'.

claims.claim: The fail-safe could not fire until the disaster was already happening.
claims.reason: This is a direct consequence of the Hi-Hi probe being set above the lowest point of the wall, as stated in IPOC pp. 16, 19-20.

claims.claim: December fourteenth, four thirty-nine in the morning. Pump two shuts itself down
claims.reason: IPOC p. 16 and data point confirm Unit #2 shut down automatically at 04:39 on Dec 14, 2005.

claims.claim: its gauge reads over six feet of room to spare.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 16 states indicated level was 1591.6 ft, meaning 5.4 ft below the 1597 ft wall, not 'over six feet'.

claims.claim: Pump one keeps going.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 16 states Unit #1 was shut down manually at 05:15, implying it continued pumping after Unit #2 stopped at 04:39.

claims.claim: On the mountain, in the dark, water is already finding the top of the wall at its lowest panel. Panel seventy-two.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 19 confirms water was going over the 1597 wall by 5:15 AM; FERC p. 103 confirms Panel 72 was the low point.

claims.claim: Right where the wet spots were.
claims.reason: FERC p. 103 confirms Cooper saw wet spots at Panel 72, the low point.

claims.claim: Water over rockfill is a saw. It found the loose rock behind the wall and began to carve.
claims.reason: Timeline event 2005-12-14 ~05:00-05:15 and data point confirm rockfill erosion due to overtopping.

claims.claim: At five fifteen, a human being finally stopped the last pump — an operator at a different dam, following a phone instruction from Saint Louis.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 16 and timeline event 2005-12-14 ~05:00-05:15 confirm Unit #1 shut down manually at 05:15 by Bagnell Dam operator on St. Louis instructions.

claims.claim: At that same minute, the wall at panel seventy-two let go.
claims.reason: IPOC p. 17 states initial breach formed at approximately 5:15 AM; FERC p. 103 confirms Panel 72 was the low point.

claims.claim: The gap tore itself six hundred fifty feet wide.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 5, 17; damfailures.org data point.

claims.claim: Four thousand three hundred fifty acre-feet — a lake — left the mountain in twenty-five minutes.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 5, 17; damfailures.org data point.

claims.claim: A wall of water, rock, and shredded forest went down Proffit Mountain at the valley below.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 5, 17; FERC p. 138.

claims.claim: Lisa held the baby.
claims.reason: Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020.

claims.claim: The five-year-old's bedroom filled before he could stand.
claims.reason: Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020.

claims.claim: The water carried them a quarter of a mile.
claims.reason: Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020.

claims.claim: in December.
claims.reason: Timeline event 2005-12-14.

claims.claim: They lived. All five of them.
claims.reason: Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020.

claims.claim: The five-year-old, Tanner, came closest.
claims.reason: Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020.

claims.claim: Two hours of resuscitation.
claims.reason: Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020.

claims.claim: So cold that warming him left burns needing skin grafts.
claims.reason: Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020.

claims.claim: A seven-month-old baby survived a quarter-mile ride through a flood that moved boulders.
claims.reason: Deseret News 12/26/2005; MBC Pathway 2020; IPOC pp. 5, 17.

claims.claim: The plant had an emergency call list, and Jerry Toops — the park superintendent — was on it.
claims.reason: FERC pp. 133-134.

claims.claim: At six thirty, they worked down the list and called his house.
claims.reason: FERC pp. 133-134.

claims.claim: There was no house.
claims.reason: FERC p. 134; Deseret News 12/26/2005.

claims.claim: The investigation took a year.
claims.reason: IPOC and FERC reports published in 2006, following a Dec 2005 breach.

claims.claim: Sensors nobody re-anchored.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 8, 109.

claims.claim: A software offset instead of a repair.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 14, 21.

claims.claim: Warning probes wired to stay silent.
claims.reason: FERC p. 63.

claims.claim: A fail-safe set above the top of a sinking wall.
claims.reason: IPOC pp. 16, 19-20; FERC p. 14.

claims.claim: Ameren paid fifteen million dollars to federal regulators.
claims.reason: STLPR 10-year retrospective; FERC consent docs.

claims.claim: a record for dam safety.
claims.reason: STLPR 10-year retrospective; FERC consent docs (as stated in timeline).

claims.claim: It paid roughly one hundred eighty million more to the state of Missouri.
claims.reason: STLPR 10-year retrospective.

claims.claim: They rebuilt the reservoir in solid concrete.
claims.reason: STLPR 10-year retrospective.

claims.claim: The new instruments cross-check each other.
claims.reason: The brief details the old system's flaws but does not explicitly describe the cross-checking features of the new instrumentation.

claims.claim: The new rim gives water somewhere to go.
claims.reason: The brief notes the old dam lacked an emergency spillway but does not explicitly describe the overflow features of the new dam.

claims.claim: It went back online in twenty ten.
claims.reason: STLPR 10-year retrospective.

claims.claim: The Toops family moved away from the park.
claims.reason: Unverifiable claims section notes the Toops family relocated in May 2006.

claims.claim: The shut-ins filled with swimmers again.
claims.reason: Johnson's Shut-Ins State Park was rebuilt and reopened in phases from 2007.

claims.claim: A disaster with no dead.
claims.reason: The brief confirms all five Toops family members survived the flood.

claims.claim: The computer did exactly what it was told.
claims.reason: The PLC was programmed with a 0.4 ft offset and continued pumping Unit #1 based on indicated levels, even as the reservoir overtopped.

claims.claim: The sensors reported faithfully from where they lay — pipes that had drifted out of place.
claims.reason: Sensors reported ~4.2 ft low, not 'faithfully,' though they were in drifted pipes.

claims.claim: Somebody saw Niagara Falls and typed point four feet into a config file.
claims.reason: Brief documents 'Niagara Falls' overtopping on 9/25/2005 and a subsequent 0.4 ft software offset on 9/27/2005.

claims.claim: We are building more of these plants now.
claims.reason: General knowledge confirms a global trend of building more pumped-hydro storage for renewable grids.

claims.claim: Run by remote.
claims.reason: Taum Sauk was operated by remote control, and this is a common feature of modern pumped-hydro plants.
